nameStory: The Common Carpet moth gets its name from the intricate striped and banded patterns on its wings that resemble the geometric designs found on traditional woven carpets. The alternating light and dark bands create a textile-like appearance that early naturalists thought looked just like the decorative floor coverings in their homes.
description: The Common Carpet is a small to medium-sized moth with distinctively striped wings that create a carpet-like pattern. Its forewings range from grey to nearly black, decorated with prominent white bands that give it a bold striped appearance. With a wingspan of about 1 to 1.2 inches, this night-flying moth is often drawn to porch lights and windows during the warmer months. The hindwings are typically paler grey with similar white striping, though less pronounced than on the forewings.

idTips.label: Striped Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive alternating light and dark bands across the forewings - grey at the base, followed by a brown band, then an almost pure white band, and finally dark brown-grey at the wing tips with a grey line running through it

idTips.label: Wing Size and Shape
idTips.description: Wings span about 1 to 1.2 inches when fully spread, with forewings that feel papery and delicate when gently touched (if found deceased)

idTips.label: Color Variation
idTips.description: Northern populations tend to be paler overall, while southern ones are often darker; the white bands can vary in width and sometimes appear broken or reduced

idTips.label: Hindwing Appearance
idTips.description: Hindwings are noticeably paler grey than the forewings, with white bands that are less bold and contrasting than those on the front wings

idTips.label: Night Activity
idTips.description: Active only at night and strongly attracted to artificial lights - you'll likely spot them fluttering around porch lights or pressed against illuminated windows

habitat: Look for Common Carpet moths in areas where bedstraw plants grow, as this is where their caterpillars feed. They're found in open woodlands, meadows, gardens, roadsides, and forest edges throughout New England. You're most likely to encounter the adults around outdoor lights in suburban and rural areas, especially near fields or woodland borders.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May, with the first generation starting their flight season. Look for them at porch lights on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August, when both first and second generations may be flying. This is the best time to observe them at lights.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be seen into September, especially from the second brood. Activity decreases as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters as a pupa, hidden in soil or leaf litter until the following spring.

funFact: This moth is essentially a living compass for climate - northern populations have evolved to be much paler than their southern cousins, possibly to help them blend in with the lighter-colored lichens and bark found in cooler regions!
confusionNotes: The Common Carpet's bold striping makes it fairly distinctive among New England moths, but it could be confused with other carpet moths in the same family. Remember the specific pattern: grey base, brown band, white band, then dark outer edge with a grey line - like reading the layers of a geological formation across the wing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'Common' Carpet, this European native is actually a relatively recent arrival to North America, having expanded its range across the northern United States and Canada. The 'carpet' name comes from 18th-century naturalists who named many similar moths after household textiles.
compareHints: Since this is the only Epirrhoe species regularly found in New England, compare it to other carpet moths in the Geometridae family by looking for its specific three-band pattern - most other carpets have more complex zigzag or wavy patterns rather than these clean alternating stripes. The white bands are usually more pronounced and regular than in related species.
